questions.question: A circle graph is divided into 10 equal sectors. 4 of those sectors are shaded green and the other 6 are white. The 10 sectors together make the whole circle. What is the central angle of the whole green part?
questions.explain: Go quantity to percent to angle: 4 out of 10 is 0.4 = 40%, and 40% of 360° is 0.4 × 360° = 144°. The usual trap is writing 40% as 40°; a percent is a share of 360°, not a number of degrees.

questions.question: A circle graph is divided into 8 equal sectors. 3 of them are shaded blue. Using the whole circle as 8 equal parts, what central angle should the blue part have?
questions.explain: 3 out of 8 is 3 ÷ 8 = 0.375 = 37.5%, so the angle is 0.375 × 360° = 135°. Do not stop at 37.5 and call it degrees, and do not give the size of just one sector (45°) — the blue part is three sectors.

questions.question: A circle graph is divided into 20 equal sectors. 5 of them are shaded red. What central angle does the red part take up?
questions.explain: 5 out of 20 is 1/4 = 0.25 = 25%, and 0.25 × 360° = 90°. Watch two traps: 18° is only one of the 20 sectors, and 25° would be copying the percent straight into degrees.

questions.question: A circle graph is divided into 5 equal sectors. Exactly 1 sector is shaded yellow. What central angle belongs to the yellow sector?
questions.explain: 1 out of 5 is 0.2 = 20%, so the angle is 0.2 × 360° = 72°. A 20° sector would be far too thin — the percent has to be multiplied by 360° before it becomes an angle.

questions.question: Emma got an $80 gift card for the Vancouver bookstore and spent $28 of it on graphic novels. She is making a circle graph of her spending. What central angle should the graphic-novel sector have?
questions.explain: First make the percent: 28 ÷ 80 = 0.35 = 35%. Then turn it into an angle: 0.35 × 360° = 126°. The common slip is drawing 35% as a 35° sector instead of multiplying by 360°.

questions.question: One sector of a circle graph is 0.15 of the whole circle. What central angle should that sector be drawn with?
questions.explain: A decimal share is multiplied by the full turn: 0.15 × 360° = 54°. Two traps to avoid — reading 0.15 as 15%, then drawing 15°, and multiplying by 36 instead of 360.

questions.question: In a survey of 40 students at a Kelowna middle school, 9 said hockey is their favourite sport. On a circle graph of the results, what central angle should the hockey sector have?
questions.explain: 9 ÷ 40 = 0.225 = 22.5%, and 0.225 × 360° = 81°. The percent 22.5 is not the angle, and the raw count 9 is not the angle either — always multiply the share by 360°.

questions.question: A sector of a circle graph must show 65% of the total. Which line of work correctly finds its central angle?
questions.explain: Change the percent to a decimal, then take that share of the full turn: 0.65 × 360° = 234°. Percent and degrees are different units, so 65% can never be drawn as 65°.

questions.question: Noah tracked his $240 summer allowance. He spent $30 of it at the snack bar and is showing the whole $240 on a circle graph. What central angle should the snack-bar sector have?
questions.explain: Two steps: 30 ÷ 240 = 0.125 = 12.5%, then 0.125 × 360° = 45°. Neither the percent (12.5) nor the dollars (30) can be used as degrees — only the share times 360° gives the angle.

questions.question: Maya is drawing a circle graph of how her class travels to school. Bus riders are 60% of the class, so she sets her protractor and draws a 60° sector for them. Which statement describes her mistake and the fix?
options: The 60° sector is fine, since a 60% share is drawn as a 60° angle
The bus sector should be 216°, since 0.60 × 360° = 216°; the percent must be taken out of 360° before drawing
The bus sector should be 108°, since 0.60 × 180° = 108°
The bus sector should be 300°, since 360° − 60° = 300°
questions.explain: A whole circle graph is 360°, so 60% of it is 0.60 × 360° = 216° — more than half the circle. Copying the percent into the protractor as 60° is the most common error, and it makes the biggest group look tiny.

questions.question: A Grade 7 class made a circle graph of how students get to school. Walking is 22%, biking is 18%, and car is 15%. Everyone else takes the bus. What central angle should the bus sector have?
questions.explain: First find the missing percent: 100% − (22% + 18% + 15%) = 45%. Then 0.45 × 360° = 162°. Drawing 45° instead of 162° is the classic mix-up of percent with degrees.

questions.question: A school recycling audit in Victoria collected 50 items. Of these, 15 were plastic bottles. The class wants a circle graph of all 50 items. What central angle should the plastic-bottle sector be?
questions.explain: 15 ÷ 50 = 0.3 = 30%, and 0.3 × 360° = 108°. Remember the order quantity to percent to angle — stopping at 30 and drawing 30° would make the plastic slice look about three times too small.
